graph-memory.heading: What is the graph remembering?
graph-memory.text: The discussions describe several different jobs for connected memory. A news graph links people, companies and stories over time. A conversation graph retains speaker-attributed opinions. A shared agent graph records discoveries and useful routes through work. They all preserve connections, but the material being remembered and the person using it differ.

graph-memory.heading: Memory for an agent, or understanding for a person?
graph-memory.text: The repository-learning example shifts the purpose again: a graph can help a developer understand concepts and architectural choices in agent-built code. That is a different goal from giving an agent reusable operational context. This guide keeps those applications separate rather than treating every graph as the same memory system.

agent-continuity.heading: What persists when a runtime ends?
agent-continuity.text: One approach uses fresh agents for bounded tasks and carries useful context forward. Another puts personality, authorised access and tools in a persistent record layer, then creates compute for each turn. Both separate continuity of work from keeping one long-running agent session alive.

agent-continuity.heading: A persistent computer is a different tradeoff
agent-continuity.text: The archive also considers giving an assistant its own continuing computer. Pete describes capability and convenience benefits alongside cost and isolation tradeoffs, while disposable workers allow bursts of bounded work. These are competing deployment choices and tentative assessments, not a single agreed architecture or a verified comparison of suppliers.

code-first-workflows.heading: Preserve a route once it is understood
code-first-workflows.text: A recurring proposal is to use agents while discovering how to do something, then encode the repeatable parts in software. The distinction is between open-ended exploration and recurring execution: discovering sources or a remedy can require judgement, while repeating a settled route may not.

code-first-workflows.heading: Where judgement remains in the workflow
code-first-workflows.text: Code-first does not remove models from the process. The pipeline examples place agents at bounded classification, routing or transformation steps and pass structured results back to code. The source discussions argue for clearer control and less repeated inference; they do not establish that every business task already has a deterministic solution.

human-review.heading: Give the reviewer something inspectable
human-review.text: Review depends on more than a polished final answer. The archive describes intermediate spreadsheets, formulas and other work products that expose how an outcome was produced. Other discussions move interface design toward checking results, finding errors and making corrections.

human-review.heading: Match the checkpoint to the work
human-review.text: Several sources favour short, reviewable increments so people can steer decisions discovered during implementation. One discussion also distinguishes unattended multi-hour work from a small visual edit, where immediate delivery and human judgement may be more useful than a long verification loop. The common concern is retaining direction, not applying an identical review ceremony to every task.

shared-work-layers.heading: Shared work does not require a shared runtime
shared-work-layers.text: The workspace discussions bring people, agents, tasks, documents and files into a common collaboration layer while allowing separate agent runtimes. The problem being addressed is continuity and visibility across many sessions, rather than making every worker use the same underlying agent.

shared-work-layers.heading: Different views onto the same records
shared-work-layers.text: A related proposal uses one authenticated record layer for canvases, task views, voice clients and agent runtimes. Identity-separated workspaces and permissions are part of that design. These discussions describe an architectural approach; they are not independent evidence that every interface or external agent already interoperates with it.
